# The Burning of the Khandava Forest <note>Section 227 and 228</note>
## Adi Parva

Arjuna, becoming very impatient, countered that rain with his arrows. When <term>Shatakratu</term> <gloss>Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices</gloss>, the subduer of <term>Paka</term> <gloss>a demon</gloss>, saw his efforts being rendered fruitless, he further increased the downpour. The subduer of Paka sent forth rain with arrows of great velocity, causing a dissolution while delighting his own side. <margin>828</margin> Then, lifting with his hands a great peak from Mount Mandara with its trees, <term>Chakra</term> <gloss>Indra, the wielder of the discus</gloss> hurled it, desiring to kill the son of Pandu.

Then Arjuna, with swift, burning-tipped, crested arrows, shattered the peak of the mountain into a thousand pieces. The appearance of the mountain as it was being destroyed shone like the sky scattering away with its sun, moon, and planets. By that great mountain falling upon the forest, the creatures dwelling in <term>Khandava</term> <gloss>the forest name</gloss> were struck and killed by its peaks.

Thus ends the two-hundred and twenty-seventh chapter in the Burning of the Khandava Forest section of the <term>Adi Parva</term> <gloss>the first book</gloss>, concerning the battle between the gods, Krishna, and Arjuna.

***

Vaisampayana said: Terrified by the fall of the mountain, the dwellers of Khandava—the <term>Danavas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, <term>Rakshasas</term> <gloss>ogres</gloss>, <term>Nagas</term> <gloss>serpents</gloss>, and forest-dwelling trees—were distraught. <margin>829</margin> Mighty elephants, tigers, and maned lions, along with various classes of beings, abandoned their homes in agitation. They looked upon that forest fire, rising with weapons raised in anger; it stood as if agitated by the sound of uprooting. Seeing the forest burning in many ways, and Krishna with weapons raised, they let out a fierce roar. By that terrible roar and the roar of <term>Vibhavasu</term> <gloss>the Fire-god</gloss>, the entire sky rumbled as if with ominous storm clouds.

Then <term>Keshava</term> <gloss>Krishna</gloss> of mighty arms hurled his great, fierce discus, brilliant with the splendor of solar fire, for their destruction. <margin>830</margin> Those small species, along with the <term>Danavas</term> and night-wanderers, were caught by it; all were cut down by the hundreds and fell into the fire in an instant. There, those <term>Daityas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss> were seen being torn apart by Krishna’s discus, smeared with fat and blood like clouds at twilight.

The descendant of <term>Vrishni</term> <gloss>Krishna</gloss> moved like <term>Kala</term> <gloss>Time or Death</gloss> itself, O Bharata, slaying thousands of <term>Pisachas</term> <gloss>flesh-eating spirits</gloss>, <term>Nagas</term>, and beasts in the flames. Wonderful and marvelous was the discus of Krishna, the slayer of enemies; after cutting through many creatures, it returned to his hand again and again. <margin>831</margin> While he was thus slaying the <term>Pisachas</term>, serpents, and <term>Rakshasas</term>, the form of that Soul of all beings became extremely fierce.

Among all the assembled gods, there was none who could be the victor over Krishna and the son of Pandu in battle. When the gods were unable to protect the strength of those beings or quench the forest fire, they turned their backs. <term>Shatakratu</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>, seeing the immortals turning away, became delighted, O King, praising Keshava and Arjuna.

When the gods had retreated, an incorporeal voice of deep resonance spoke, addressing <term>Shatakratu</term>: "Your friend <term>Takshaka</term>, the best of serpents, is not present here; at the time of the burning of Khandava, he has gone to Kurukshetra. <margin>832</margin> Nor is it possible to conquer these two in battle by any means, O <term>Vasava</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>. Understand these words of mine regarding Vasudeva and Arjuna. These two are <term>Nara</term> and <term>Narayana</term> <gloss>the ancient twin sages/deities</gloss>, the former gods famous in heaven. You yourself know what their heroism and prowess are. These two, unassailable and undefeated in battle, cannot be conquered even by all the worlds; they are the most excellent of ancient sages. They are most worthy of worship by all the gods and demons, <term>Yakshas</term>, <term>Rakshasas</term>, <term>Gandharvas</term>, humans, <term>Kinnaras</term>, and <term>Pannagas</term>. Therefore, O <term>Vasava</term>, you should depart along with the gods; see this destruction of Khandava as something ordained by destiny." <margin>833</margin>

Having heard these words and knowing them to be true, the Lord of the Immortals cast aside his anger and resentment and then departed for heaven.

<summary>Indra attempts to stop the burning of Khandava Forest by hurling mountain peaks, but Arjuna destroys them. Krishna uses his divine discus to slaughter the fleeing creatures, and a heavenly voice eventually persuades Indra to withdraw by revealing the divine identities of Krishna and Arjuna as Nara and Narayana.</summary>
<keywords>Indra, Arjuna, Krishna, Khandava Forest, Nara-Narayana, Takshaka, divine weapons, Agni, Sudarshana Chakra</keywords>
